newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian study monitors 40,000 women's health.
newsitem.headline: Australian study monitors 40,000 women's health.

text.p: A quarter of young Australian women are underweight and many suffer stress, while middle-aged women are becoming more obsese and suffer hypertension, according to early data from a study of 40,000 women.
The 20-year study started in 1995 plans to track the health of the women, aged 18-22, 45-49 and 70-74, looking at factors such as body weight, healthcare and stress.

The Australian Longitudinal Study of Women's Health by researchers from the universities of Newcastle and Queensland, will also attempt to determine the health impact of a range of social, emotional and physical factors.
"We are really taking a global view of women's health," project manager Wendy Brown told Reuters on Wednesday.
Body weight was a key area of the study to assess whether weight problems have a long-term impact on health, Brown said.
Middle-aged women were becoming more obese and suffering related problems such as diabetes and hypertension. By contrast, an increasing proportion of young women were underweight.
Brown said these young women could suffer long-term effects such as interrupted menstrual cycle, early menopause and osteoporosis -- problems seen in very thin elite athletes.
Younger women had been questioned about their aspirations, to see if these were fulfilled or changed over time.

"Something like 90 percent of them want to be married, they want to have two children, they want to have more education and they want to be in the workforce," said Brown, adding that many younger women reported much more stress.
The study found 60 percent of young and middle-aged women felt under pressure daily or several times a week. This compared with 27 percent of the older women.
The study found some health problems occur less frequently in the older age group, including headaches and tiredness.
It also documented a high rate of menstrual symptoms among mid-life women, which disrupt their employment, social life, relationships and family life.
Australian women currently live longer than men, but Brown said it was possible the pattern of mortality among women could begin to change with increased aspirations.
"There has to be some toll on women taking on all of these roles," she said.
